name: CBT for BDD

lead: CBT for BDD is a structured psychotherapy for people intensely preoccupied with a perceived flaw in their appearance. The payoff is less time and distress spent on the flaw and a steadier, more confident self-image. It is the best-studied psychological treatment for the condition.

Sessions combine education about BDD, challenging appearance-related beliefs, exposure to feared situations while holding back rituals like mirror checking or reassurance seeking, and in some programs mindfulness and attention retraining. A 2016 meta-analysis of randomized trials and a 2019 trial against supportive psychotherapy examined its effect on BDD symptoms, and it has been tested in adolescents and in app-based formats. Trials measure symptoms, not looks.

paras: People work with a trained therapist in regular sessions over several months, practising exposure exercises and tracking rituals between sessions. App-based and digital versions exist for people with limited access to specialists. It is sometimes raised as an alternative or complement to cosmetic procedures.

Therapy has no drug-type side effects, though it can be emotionally demanding because it involves facing feared situations. Access to clinicians trained in BDD is limited, which is one reason digital versions are being studied. A qualified clinician is the route to diagnosis.

angle.text: CBT for BDD uses exposure and response prevention to cut checking behaviours and challenge appearance beliefs, so people spend less energy on perceived flaws and carry themselves with more confidence. It is the best-studied talk therapy for BDD, with trials measuring symptom reduction rather than looks.

lead: Cognitive-behavioral therapy for body dysmorphic disorder (CBT-BDD) is a form of psychotherapy designed for people with body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), a condition marked by preoccupation with a perceived flaw in appearance. Treatment typically combines psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring, exposure with response prevention (ERP), and in some programs mindfulness and perceptual retraining.[1][2]

It is described in the research literature as the best-studied psychological treatment for BDD.[3] A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials examined its effect on validated BDD measures,[3] and a 2019 randomized trial compared therapist-delivered CBT with supportive psychotherapy.[4] Researchers have also tested app-based and digital versions and adolescent programs.[5][6][7]

In looksmaxxing communities, BDD is discussed as a condition that can overlap with appearance-focused self-improvement, and therapy is sometimes raised as an alternative or complement to cosmetic procedures. Wikipedia notes that many people with BDD seek cosmetic or dermatologic treatment that typically does not relieve their distress.[1]

paras: BDD is classified in the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders group in the DSM-5.[1] People with BDD spend substantial time thinking about a perceived defect and often perform repetitive behaviors such as mirror checking, reassurance seeking, comparing and camouflaging.[1]

A modular CBT program described by Wilhelm and colleagues includes psychoeducation and case formulation, cognitive restructuring, exposure and ritual (response) prevention, and mindfulness and perceptual retraining, according to Wikipedia's summary.[1] In ERP, a person gradually faces feared appearance-related situations, such as going without camouflage, while refraining from the usual checking or avoidance rituals.[3]

Enrico Morselli described the condition as dysmorphophobia in 1886; DSM-III recognised it in 1980 as an atypical somatoform disorder, DSM-III-R renamed it body dysmorphic disorder in 1987, and DSM-5 in 2013 placed it in the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders group and noted the muscle dysmorphia subtype [1]. Wikipedia describes muscle dysmorphia as mostly affecting men and involving a perception of the muscular body as too small, which is relevant to physique-focused communities [1].

The modular CBT manual by Wilhelm and colleagues, published in 2011, is the programme most often described as the template for CBT-BDD, with psychoeducation and case formulation, cognitive restructuring, exposure and ritual prevention, and mindfulness and perceptual retraining [1]. Wikipedia lists both CBT and SSRIs as treatments considered effective, citing a 2016 meta-analysis and a Cochrane review [1][8].

In the 2019 trial, therapist-delivered CBT-BDD was described as a modular, skills-based treatment. Its components were psychoeducation, case formulation, goal setting around personally valued activities, motivational enhancement, cognitive restructuring, exposure and ritual prevention, mindfulness and attention retraining, and later modules on beliefs about appearance, self-acceptance, self-esteem and self-compassion. [4][9] Optional modules addressed particular symptoms, including the urge to seek surgical or dermatological treatment. [9] Relapse prevention was covered in the final sessions. [9]

The course ran as 22 individual 60-minute sessions over 24 weeks, weekly at first and then spaced further apart, with two booster sessions at one and three months for people who had responded. [9] People in the trial were adults with a primary BDD diagnosis and at least moderate severity on the BDD-YBOCS, a clinician-rated scale from 0 to 48; the average age was about 34 and roughly three quarters of participants were women. [9]

For people interested in how they look, practitioners describe the aim of this therapy as reducing the time and distress taken up by appearance preoccupation, checking and avoidance, so that appearance concerns occupy less of daily life and other goals, relationships and activities become easier to pursue. [3][9] Because it targets the preoccupation, clinicians describe it as something that can be used before, instead of, or alongside cosmetic treatment decisions. [1][2]

A coach-supported smartphone app called Perspectives covers psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring, exposure with response prevention, mindfulness, attention retraining and relapse prevention, and was tested in an initial randomized waitlist-controlled trial.[5] An earlier pilot tested a digital CBT service for BDD.[10]
Adolescent-specific CBT has been examined in a case series and in a follow-up of a randomized trial.[6][11]

A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of CBT for BDD, covering published and unpublished trials to November 2015, used validated BDD measures as primary outcomes and depression and insight as secondary outcomes.[3]

The 2019 JAMA Psychiatry trial randomised 120 adults at two sites, Massachusetts General Hospital and Rhode Island Hospital, to CBT-BDD (61) or supportive psychotherapy (59); each arm had 22 weekly one-hour sessions over 24 weeks with booster sessions for responders [4]. Symptom reduction favoured CBT-BDD at the Rhode Island site but not significantly at the Massachusetts General site, depression, insight and functioning improved in both arms, and among week-24 completers, response rates (30 percent or more symptom reduction) were 84.6 and 83.3 percent for CBT-BDD at the two sites versus 69.2 and 45.5 percent for supportive psychotherapy [4]. Gains were maintained through six months of follow-up in both groups [4]. A separate analysis examined predictors of response to CBT for BDD,[12] and another proposed empirical definitions of treatment response and remission in BDD.[13]

In adolescents, a follow-up study of 26 participants who had received CBT for BDD examined whether treatment gains were maintained over a longer period,[6] and an earlier case series reported on CBT in adolescents.[11]

The coach-supported app trial randomised 80 adults to 12 weeks of the Perspectives app with bachelor's-level coach support or to a waitlist; end-of-treatment symptom severity was lower in the app group (mean 16.8 versus 26.7, d = 1.44), with improvements in insight, depression, quality of life and functioning; because the control was a waitlist, the trial does not separate CBT effects from expectancy or coach contact.[5]

Treatment guidance describes selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors as the main medication option for BDD, and CBT as the main psychological option, with the choice depending on severity, preference and availability. [2][8] An international consensus statement synthesised the pharmacological and psychological evidence for the condition and discusses combining the two. [2] A 2009 Cochrane review of pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy for BDD is among the sources that report both approaches as beneficial in randomised trials. [8]

Wikipedia reports that people with BDD frequently pursue cosmetic surgery or dermatology and that this typically does not relieve their distress; it recommends that cosmetic surgeons and psychiatrists work together to screen for BDD.[1] Prevalence estimates cited there range from about 2-3 percent in the general population to a higher figure in a global meta-analysis, and about 24 percent among people seeking plastic surgery.[1]

In appearance-focused communities, BDD is discussed alongside the question of how much dissatisfaction is a reasonable motivation for self-improvement and how much is a clinical condition. Wikipedia reports that people with BDD frequently pursue cosmetic procedures without relief of their distress, and that screening in cosmetic practice is recommended [1]. Clinicians describe CBT for BDD as a treatment aimed at the preoccupation and rituals rather than at the appearance itself [3].

timeline.event: DSM-III-R renames the condition body dysmorphic disorder.[1]
DSM-5 places BDD in the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders group.[1]
Systematic review and meta-analysis of CBT randomized trials for BDD published.[3]
